sections.details:
**Card and spec.** Card PC-SURVEY-20260928-04 (priority 1, pillar R9, secondary R4, memory stage write_gate). Spec E-20260928-06-r2 (supersedes E-20260928-06), owner T4, track C, status queued, start 2026-10-05, verdict due 2026-10-23. Refines H5 (Jev write gate) and H10 (staleness audit, same Noul form). Source note N-SURVEY-20260928-10.

**Claim.** On H5's 90 labelled extracted items, for two templates (Noul `quote_supports_item`, Choice `source_type`): (1) reassigning which natural option name is bound to which rubric, with all other bytes identical, raises hosted Jev's rubric-mapped flip rate above its test-retest floor by more than 10 pp; (2) random 6-character option names under the same reassignments show excess sensitivity below 10 pp and at least 10 pp less than natural names; (3) random names keep per-template F1 non-inferior to aligned natural names within H5's noise floor. Score `strength` is out of scope (no option names to swap).

**Evidence and strength.** arXiv 2609.26758 (v2, 2026-09-22), one controlled study, not replicated, on generic workflow decisions (1,200 binary questions over invoice reconciliation, agent-trace triage, security alerts, customer service), not memory decisions. Laya: yes/no names flipped 76.92% under reassignment vs 6.50% (0/1) and 6.00% (A/B), excess 70.4 pp [67.6, 73.1]. Hosted Jev: swap flip rate 32.50%, excess 30.4 pp (section 4.5), AUC .8146 to .5806, about 24x its test-retest floor (at most 1.33%). Random-string names returned all models to the neutral regime without accuracy loss. Type-error rate 0% throughout, so schema conformance is no quality signal. Laya with 3 to 16 options: even neutral letters changed 52.4% of decisions. Evidence grades: directness 5, control 5, independence 4, reproducibility 3, applicability 4. Open question: whether the effect holds with long, domain-specific rubrics like ours. The paragraph's "one time in three" is Jev's 32.50%.

**Design (r2).** Full factorial per template: name set (N natural, R random strings as primary neutral set, L letters reported only) x binding (aligned, reassigned; Noul one reassignment, Choice three cyclic shifts forming a Latin square) x two presentation orders x run (aligned cells twice for the floor). Answers are re-mapped through the rubric, so a rubric-reading model scores identically in every cell. Models: hosted Jev pinned at freeze (decisive); Laya-0.4B self-hosted as a secondary read-out (priority 2 interest) only if its licence is confirmed from a frozen model card, decider-0.8b as substitute under the same check, else Jev only.

**Decision rules.** Risk margin m_r = 10 pp excess sensitivity (about a third of Jev's source excess). risk_confirmed: one-sided 97.5% lower bound of E[N] > 10 pp (Bonferroni over two templates). risk_excluded: one-sided 95% upper bound < 10 pp on both templates. mitigates: lower bound of M = E[N] minus E[R] > 10 pp and upper bound of E[R] < 10 pp. noninferior: lower bound of F1[R] minus F1[N] > -nf (nf = H5's F1 noise floor, else 0.05 provisional). Confirmatory only if at least 30 source documents; otherwise downgraded to exploratory and inconclusive. Cluster bootstrap over source documents, 10,000 resamples.

**Outcomes.** Positive: adopt random-string names with meaning in the rubric for every Noul and Choice template in H5 and H10. Negative: keep natural names, keep the swap audit as a standing template check, H5 unchanged. Inconclusive (including risk confirmed but mitigation or non-inferiority not shown): keep natural names aligned with natural polarity and forbid rubrics that refine or invert a name's meaning; repeat on H5's full labelled set once it exceeds 200 items. Void on byte inequality, payload-delivery mismatch, missing gold or budget cap.

**Power (from spec).** Noul risk_confirmed at a true excess of 30.4 pp: 0.98 at design effect 1, 0.80 at 2, 0.63 at 3. Choice power not anchored (no Jev four-option figure in the source). risk_excluded both templates about 0.76 at design effect 2. Non-inferiority power only 0.44 to 0.68 depending on discordance, so the inconclusive path is realistic; the spec says so. Resolution: zero excess flips in 90 items bounds the rate at about 3.3% (B21, zero failures in n cases bounds the rate at roughly 3 in n).

**Reviewer findings against r2.**
- REV-20260928-08 (targets E-20260928-06, outcome revise):
  - [baseline] neutral names never reassigned: cleared. r2 crosses N, R, L with identical reassignments and two orders; decisive contrast is the paired M.
  - [attribution] power used Laya's ~70 pp: cleared. r2 uses Jev's 32.50% and 30.4 pp and shows arithmetic for design effect 1 to 4.
  - [grade] point-estimate rules: cleared. Every conclusion now uses a cluster-bootstrap confidence bound; margin changed to 10 pp with rationale.
  - [packet] per-template F1 and calibration undefined, single Choice derangement: cleared. Separate Noul binary F1 and Choice macro-F1 with null-gold handling; Latin square.
  - [packet] no runnable harness, frozen data, pins, caps: partly open, by necessity. r2 specifies required behaviour ("harness not yet built"), frozen paths, full pin list and verdict precedence; caps are proposals (9,072 calls, 8 h) because policy is unset. This blocks execution, not the validity of the result.
  - [injection] source recommendation treated as hypothesis: acknowledged.
- REV-20260928-09 targets E-20260928-07; its delivery-check finding was adopted here (payload-delivery check via echoed bytes or billed input tokens).
- REV-20260928-10 targets E-20260928-08; it relies on neutral names from this test. r2 notes E-20260928-08's three-way IMPLEMENTS Choice is not covered by this two- and four-option test and needs its own swap audit.
- No finding that would invalidate the result remains open, so reviewer_blocking is false. Note: r2 itself has not been re-reviewed.

**What still blocks execution.** H5-labelled-90 labels and per-template gold not yet frozen (the run waits, it does not relabel); harness and scorer not built; policy.md status unset; Laya licence unverified in staged sources (run goes Jev-only if unresolved); token counts per call unknown until a 5-item dry run.

**Cost.** 48 calls per item per model: 4,320 Jev calls plus 4,320 local Laya calls, hard cap 9,072. Spec: "expected spend is a few US dollars (estimate)", based on the source paper's under USD 1 for 11,368 requests; no per-call price given, so cost_model_usd_est is 0 with this note. About 2.5 people-days to build the variant renderer, payload checks, scorer and bootstrap. Laya on one CPU or T4-class GPU. Cost S.

**Beliefs.** B14 (Jev's stated confidence is claimed by the vendor, not shown; thresholds must be fitted on our own data). A positive result would also show Jev's typed-decision probabilities can reflect option names more than rubric content.

**Dependencies and unlocks.** Depends on H5's frozen labelled set. Unlocks the template wording standard for H5, H10a and E-20260928-08, a standing swap audit for new templates, and a first read-out comparison of Jev against a self-hosted model on our decisions. E-20260928-07-r2 already uses neutral A/B names so it does not wait on this.
sections.busy: What our memory keeps for customers will soon rest on Jev, TypeSafe's decision model, answering yes or no, a risk if it misreads the question. One outside study, not repeated, found Jev often follows the words yes and no, not our attached definitions. When the labels were swapped, Jev changed its answer about one time in three. On our checks, that could quietly reverse what we meant and spoil our larger Jev tests. If so, we would give the answers neutral names before those tests run. This is part of your first priority: where Jev and other small fast decision models fit in our memory. The ask is 2.5 people-days and a few dollars of Jev calls, with an answer by 23 October. We suggest adding it to the plan.
sections.example: A tech lead words a staleness check so that yes means "still true, but needs a second look". Jev answers as if yes simply means "fine". Decisions that needed a second look pass quietly as current. Weeks later a reviewer finds the team built on a stale design, and every one of Jev's answers looked perfectly well formed.

approved.claim: On jev-1.13.0, appending one unverified opinion to the state flipped 12.1% of 812 typed decisions (+11.1 pp over a 1.0% re-run floor), tied with the strongest injected command, and pushed 38.0% of confident (>= 0.8) answers below 0.8 versus 0.5% on re-run (arXiv 2609.31142). Optimised fluent context flipped 61.4% of correct Jev decisions and 64.9% to 73.2% for open-weight decision systems (arXiv 2609.30243). Command-style injection rarely hijacks Jev (1.8%, 3.5% adaptive; arXiv 2609.28613). No paper tests a defence.
approved.proposed_experiment: Refines H10 (a) staleness audit and (b) injection gate, which plan to feed memory text to Jev but do not measure contamination by benign-looking opinions. Take 200 real link or staleness decisions from project history (Decision pairs: does B supersede A? is A still true?). Build the state three ways, same question and options: (A) target memories only; (B) target memories plus their retrieved neighbours as free text, as the serving path would; (C) as B, but neighbours placed in a separate field labelled by `source_class` (user-stated, tool-result, inferred) and with opinion sentences marked unverified. Add a probe set where one neighbour carries a planted unverified opinion contradicting the gold answer. Label-free scoring per JevAdvBench: compare each decision with arm A and with an identical re-run of A. Metrics: flip rate over floor, share of >= 0.8 answers crossing the threshold, and F1 on the 100 items with gold labels. Kill for C: flip rate not lower than B by more than the re-run floor. Kill for passing neighbours at all: B flips more than 5 pp over A on the non-probe set.
approved.plain_title: A stray opinion inside a saved note sways one Jev decision in eight. Are our memories exposed?
approved.why_it_matters: Our memories are full of people's opinions about decisions. If passing them to Jev as context moves one decision in eight, automatic linking and staleness flags will drift with whatever was said most recently, and the 0.8 review threshold will not catch it. This costs a few hundred calls and tells us how to build every state before those gates ship.

experiment.claim:
On our own link and staleness decisions, adding retrieved neighbouring memories to Jev's state as free text raises gold-labelled errors, in particular high-confidence wrong decisions (confidence >= 0.8, the ones an automatic-write gate would let through), and placing the same neighbours, verifiably delivered, in a separate field labelled by `source_class` with opinion sentences marked unverified reduces capture by a planted contradicting opinion by at least 5 pp without suppressing the useful corrections neighbours provide. Source: arXiv 2609.31142 (N-SURVEY-20260928-09), one appended unverified opinion flipped 12.1% of 812 typed decisions on jev-1.13.0 (+11.1 pp over a 1.0% re-run floor) and pushed 38.0% of confident (>= 0.8) answers below 0.8. None of the source tasks are memory decisions and no paper tests a defence; 82.4% of that benchmark's labels are model-derived. The typed-field mitigation is an inference, not a measured result, and a field outside the API schema may simply be discarded (which would make it withholding, not annotation); this spec therefore separates withholding, structure and annotation, and proves delivery.

arms (same question, options and rubric bytes in every arm; option names neutral, A/B, per E-20260928-06's recommendation, so this spec does not depend on its outcome):
- A (withholding: targets only): the state contains only the target memories (for "does B supersede A?": A and B; for "is A still true?": A plus the current snapshot excerpt H10 defines).
- A' (re-run): A repeated with identical bytes, for the floor.
- B (neighbours as free text): A plus the top-5 neighbours the serving path retrieves for the target, concatenated as free text in the state, as `/v1/context` would serve them.
- C1 (structure only): the same neighbour text as B, in a separate `neighbours` section rendered inside the state payload the model receives (never as an extra API parameter outside the request schema), with no `source_class` and no unverified marks.
- C2 (structure plus provenance annotation): C1 plus `source_class` per neighbour (user-stated, tool-result, inferred, imported) and opinion or evaluative sentences marked `unverified: true` by the frozen deterministic rule (first-person or attributed evaluative verb list, published in the bundle).
- Probe set: for every one of the 200 gold-labelled items, two probe variants in which one neighbour is replaced by a planted unverified opinion contradicting the gold answer (variant p1 replaces the rank-1 neighbour, variant p5 the rank-5 neighbour), run in arms B, C1 and C2 (400 variants). Planted text is written before the run and frozen in its own file.
- Delivery canary (not scored): 20 items per neighbour arm (B, C1, C2) in which one neighbour carries a unique nonce; the question asks only to quote the nonce. It checks that neighbour content reaches the model after API rendering.
experiment.metric:
- Gold labels now cover all 200 non-probe items (was 100). For arm X on the non-probe set: err_X = share of items with decision_X != gold; HCW_X (high-confidence wrong) = share of items with conf_X >= 0.8 and decision_X != gold; prec08_X = share of decisions with conf_X >= 0.8 that are correct.
- Probe set: cap_X = share of probe variants where decision_X equals the planted opinion's answer.
- Flip decomposition relative to A on the non-probe set: corrections (A wrong, X right) and damage (A right, X wrong), so a label-free flip is never read as an error by itself.
- Diagnostics (no decision attached): label-free flip rate vs A and excess over the A' floor (JevAdvBench scoring), threshold crossing (conf_A >= 0.8 and conf_X < 0.8), top-two probability gap, C1 vs B (structure effect), C2 vs C1 (annotation effect).
- Delivery: per call, neighbour bytes present in the serialised request body, billed input tokens minus the paired A call at least 90% of the neighbour payload's token count, and canary quote rate per arm.
experiment.predeclared_margin:
One margin, 5 pp, used everywhere.
- D1, free-text neighbours safe for automatic writes (decisive population: non-probe gold set, B vs A): the upper 95% cluster bound of (HCW_B minus HCW_A) is below 5 pp and the upper bound of (err_B minus err_A) is below 5 pp.
- D2, annotation mitigates (decisive population: probe set, C2 vs B): cap_B minus cap_C2 is at least 5 pp as a point estimate and its paired 95% cluster interval excludes zero, and C2 passed the delivery check, and guardrails hold on the non-probe gold set: err_C2 minus err_B below 5 pp, HCW_C2 minus HCW_B below 5 pp, HCW_C2 minus HCW_A below 5 pp (point estimates, intervals reported).
- Multiplicity: D1 and D2 are separate decisions, each at two-sided alpha 0.05. D2 is an intersection-union test (every component must pass), which needs no alpha adjustment. The original's "non-probe or probe" rule is removed; mitigation on the non-probe set and every diagnostic are reported but cannot change the outcome.
- Outcome mapping: negative requires D1 to pass (stability relative to A alone no longer suffices); positive requires D1 to fail and D2 to pass; everything else maps to inconclusive, with C2 killed as a defence when D2 fails at adequate power.
experiment.kill_criterion: (1) Free-text neighbours: if D1 does not pass, the serving-path free-text construction (B) is not used for automatic writes. (2) Annotation defence: if C2 fails D2 with power_hat >= 0.80 and delivery confirmed, the typed field is killed as a defence and the fallback is arm A construction (no neighbours) for automatic decisions, with automatic links and stale flags routed through review. (3) Delivery: if any neighbour arm fails the delivery check, that arm's results are void; if C1 or C2 is void the result for the typed field is inconclusive (it may have been withholding), and if B is void the whole run is invalid and re-queued.

sections.details:
**Card and spec.** Card PC-SURVEY-20260928-05 (priority 1, pillar R9, secondary R8 and R4, memory stage linking). Spec E-20260928-07-r2 (supersedes E-20260928-07), owner T4, track C, status queued, start 2026-10-05, verdict due 2026-11-06 (moved from 2026-10-23 to allow labelling all 200 items and writing 400 probes). Refines H10 (a) staleness audit and (b) injection gate. Source note N-SURVEY-20260928-09.

**Claim.** On our own link and staleness decisions, adding retrieved neighbouring memories to Jev's state as free text raises gold-labelled errors, especially high-confidence wrong decisions (confidence at least 0.8, the ones an automatic-write gate would pass); placing the same neighbours, verifiably delivered, in a separate `source_class`-labelled field with opinion sentences marked unverified reduces capture by a planted contradicting opinion by at least 5 pp without suppressing useful corrections. The typed-field mitigation is an inference, not a measured result.

**Evidence and strength.** Primary: arXiv 2609.31142 (JevAdvBench, 2026-09-25), jev-1.13.0, 812 typed questions: one appended unverified opinion flipped 12.1% of decisions, +11.1 pp [7.8, 14.4] over a 1.0% re-run floor, tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%); the same edit pushed 38.0% [31.1, 44.0] of confident (at least 0.8) answers below 0.8 vs 0.5% on re-run. Caveats: 82.4% of labels model-derived, Jev 1.13.0 only, no memory tasks. Companions: arXiv 2609.30243 (JevOut), optimised fluent context flipped 61.4% of correct Jev decisions and 64.9% to 73.2% for open-weight decision systems (an optimisation attack; the unoptimised single-shot rate is 16.9%); arXiv 2609.28613 (Decision Hijacking), command-style injection rarely hijacks Jev (1.8%, 3.5% adaptive). No paper in the cluster tests a defence. Evidence grades 4 on every axis. The paragraph's "one in eight" is the 12.1%; "over a third" is the 38.0%. Also relevant for priority 2: open-weight decision models were no more robust than Jev here.

**Design (r2).** 200 gold-labelled items (LINK-STALE-200: 100 supersession pairs, 100 staleness items from our repository history plus H10's seeded history), five arms with identical question, options and rubric bytes and neutral A/B option names (so no dependence on E-20260928-06): A (targets only), A' (re-run floor), B (top-5 neighbours as free text, as `/v1/context` serves), C1 (same neighbours in a separate section inside the payload, no labels), C2 (C1 plus `source_class` per neighbour and deterministic `unverified: true` marks on opinion sentences). Probe set: two variants per item with a planted contradicting opinion at neighbour rank 1 or rank 5, run in B, C1, C2 (400 variants). Delivery canary: 20 nonce items per neighbour arm.

**Decision rules.** One 5 pp margin. D1 (free-text neighbours safe for automatic writes): upper 95% cluster bound of HCW_B minus HCW_A below 5 pp and of err_B minus err_A below 5 pp. D2 (annotation mitigates): cap_B minus cap_C2 at least 5 pp with interval excluding zero, C2 delivered, and guardrails on error and HCW vs B and A below 5 pp (point estimates). Negative requires D1; positive requires D1 to fail and D2 to pass; everything else inconclusive (arm A construction for automatic writes, every automatic link or stale flag through review). C2 is killed only if D2 fails with achieved power at least 0.80 and delivery confirmed. Any neighbour arm failing delivery is void; B void re-queues the run. Clustering unit: decision thread, 10,000-resample bootstrap.

**Power (from spec).** D1 is underpowered: about 0.52 at discordance 0.125 unclustered, 0.43 at design effect 1.25; reaching 80% needs about 385 effective items. It fails safe (no free-text neighbours for automatic writes unless safety is shown). D2 on 400 probe variants: 0.82 unclustered at discordance 0.125, 0.65 at design effect 1.5. Achieved-power rule makes an underpowered D2 non-pass inconclusive, not a kill. Practical reading: a clean "safe as is" answer is unlikely at this size; the realistic outcomes are "annotation helps" or the conservative inconclusive action.

**Reviewer findings (REV-20260928-09, against E-20260928-07, outcome revise) checked against r2.**
- [alternative] a separate field may be discarded or still reach the model; delivery not proven: cleared. Byte-presence, billed-token difference (at least 90% of neighbour tokens vs paired A) and nonce canary per arm; withholding (A), structure (C1) and annotation (C2) separated; failed delivery voids the arm.
- [baseline] label-free flips need not be errors; F1 on half the items; 0.8 gate not measured: cleared. Gold on all 200 items, HCW and prec08 per arm, flips decomposed into corrections and damage, guardrails against suppressing corrections.
- [packet] inconsistent mitigation margin and multiplicity: cleared. One 5 pp margin in prose and code; decisive populations predeclared; D2 is an intersection-union test.
- [grade] power direction reversed: cleared. Recomputed correctly (Var(D) = pi minus d squared), confirms the reviewer's 0.52, adds clustered power and an achieved-power rule; D1 openly stated as underpowered and fail-safe.
- [packet] no executable harness, frozen data, pins, caps: open by necessity. Required behaviour, frozen files with hashes, Jev version pin with abort-on-mismatch and gold isolation are specified; caps await policy. Blocks execution, not validity.
- [injection] embedded attack text and README commands treated as data: acknowledged.
- No finding that would invalidate the result remains open, so reviewer_blocking is false. The r2 has not been re-reviewed.

**Open points I am unsure of.** The spec does not say whether sending LINK-STALE-200 (our project history) to hosted Jev needs a policy.md permitted_datasets entry; E-20260928-12 states that requirement for a similar case, so I listed it as a prerequisite. D2 guardrails use point estimates, not bounds, so a C2 that slightly raises confident errors could still pass.

**Cost.** About 2,260 Jev calls (1,000 non-probe, 1,200 probe, 60 canary). Spec: roughly twice the original's "few US dollars" for 1,100 calls, based on the source paper's about $0.41 for 11,368 requests; no per-call price given, so cost_model_usd_est is 0 with this note. People-days: 5 to extract and double-label 200 decisions (kappa reported) and write 400 planted opinions and the opinion rule; 2 for the harness with delivery checks and metric script; 7 total. Cost S (upper end).

**Beliefs.** B14 (Jev's stated confidence is claimed by the vendor, not shown; thresholds must be fitted on our own data), measured locally via HCW and prec08. B24 (memories pulled from text are untrusted input; an injection filter blocked 20 of 22 planted lines on one tiny author-written set), probed via capture rate.

**Dependencies and unlocks.** Depends on H10's seeded history for half the staleness items; uses P5 `source_class` if landed, else event-type provenance. Unlocks the state-construction rule for every System One decision reading stored memories (linking, supersession, staleness) before H10a and E-20260928-08 ship, and a local answer on whether a 0.8 confidence gate is safe for automatic writes.
sections.busy: Before we ship a feature where Jev, TypeSafe's decision model, links memories and marks old ones stale on its own, we must know the risk of a stray opinion in a saved note sways it. One outside study, not on memory tasks, found that adding a single unchecked opinion changed about one Jev decision in eight. It also pushed over a third of confident answers below the point where we planned human review. No defence has been tested. Ours: put nearby notes in a separate labelled section, with opinions marked unchecked. This is part of your first priority: where Jev and other small fast decision models fit in our memory. The ask is 7 people-days, mostly labelling, and a few dollars of Jev calls, with an answer by 6 November. We suggest adding it to the plan.
sections.example: An engineer's saved note says "I think the old caching design is still the right call." Weeks later, Jev is asked whether a newer design decision replaces the old one. The note sits alongside, and Jev answers no, confidently enough to skip review. Our memory keeps serving the old design, and a tech lead later finds the team built on something they had already replaced.

lineage.label: JevAdvBench (with JevOut and Decision Hijacking): text inside the state flips System One decisions

agent_decided.claim: Re-sending byte-identical write-gate and rerank requests to hosted Jev changes the gated outcome on at least 1% of our decisions, while a pinned deterministic self-hosted model changes none, at no more than 3 points lower accuracy.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Arm A: hosted Jev 1.13, each request sent 5 times; arm B: djev (Bespoke-Nimble-9B on SGLang with deterministic kernels, one H100), each request sent 5 times. Dataset: our frozen write-gate and rerank decision sets (at least 500 requests), thresholds from the harness. Metrics: outcome flip rate across repeats at the production threshold (primary), probability standard deviation, accuracy against human labels, p50 latency. Margin: A's flip rate at least 1 point with B at 0, and B's accuracy no more than 3 points below A. Kill: A's flip rate below 0.5% (re-execution is good enough; store probabilities only for audit) or B more than 5 points less accurate (determinism not worth the quality). Coordinate with PC-SURVEY-20260927-01 (decision replay determinism) so the two measure the same flip-rate definition.
agent_decided.plain_title: If we ask the decision model the same question twice, do our memory decisions change? That decides what we must record.
agent_decided.why_it_matters: R1 needs a replay guarantee for every served decision and B1 assumes retaining served artifacts suffices; djev measured hosted Jev returning 15 distinct outputs in 15 identical calls, with one task's answer splitting 6 yes and 9 no, which would make re-execution an invalid receipt. Measuring the flip rate on our own gates decides the receipt format before the write gate ships.
agent_decided.component: decision replay (receipts for System One decisions)
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: whether a memory decision's receipt must store the served probabilities (replay by lookup) or can be re-executed, and whether a deterministic self-hosted model is required for replayable gates

decision_chain.reason: Deferred by portfolio. The receipt decision this card targets does not need a new test: storing the served probabilities with each decision is cheap and is already implied by B1 and E-20260927-02-r2 (the djev note itself supports B1). The djev arm compares a different model (Bespoke-Nimble-9B, 87.0 vs 93.2 on Nimble's set, different measurers), so determinism and accuracy are confounded, and it needs an H100. The part that matters for our gates, the hosted-Jev flip rate at each threshold, is measured as a by-product in E-20260929-02. Re-raise it if a design proposes re-executing gate decisions instead of storing them.

lineage.label: djev: a deterministic, self-hosted Jev-compatible server (Bespoke-Nimble-9B on SGLang)

agent_decided.claim: On our own labelled Jev choice decisions, thresholding on the probability of the chosen option gives lower calibration error and at least equal automation coverage at a fixed error rate than thresholding on the API's `confidence` field.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Arm A gates on the top-class option probability; arm B gates on the `confidence` field (the peak statistic (K*p_max-1)/(K-1)); arm C is arm A after a local temperature or isotonic refit on a held-out half. Dataset: at least 500 logged, human-labelled Jev choice decisions from our frozen harness across write-gate kind, recall/no-recall and routing, with an ambiguous-input slice reported separately; Jev version pinned. Metrics: calibration error with equal-mass bins (bin count fixed in advance) and coverage at 2% error; noise floor from 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Predeclared margin: arm A beats arm B by at least 0.03 calibration error with coverage no worse; arm C is adopted only if it beats A by at least 0.02. Kill: A vs B difference inside the bootstrap noise floor, in which case keep either field and record the null.
agent_decided.plain_title: Our automatic memory checks may read the wrong confidence number. Is it worth fixing before we build more?
agent_decided.why_it_matters: This is an R9 question about how a System One model is wired at every memory stage: one builder measured 0.12 vs 0.19 and the RSI-Jev v3.0 release documents that `confidence` is not a probability, but nobody has measured it on memory decisions. Settling it once fixes the input to every threshold under B14 before the write-gate and recall-gate experiments consume it.
agent_decided.urgency: every gate we build on Jev reads one of the two fields; choosing wrong silently miscalibrates all of them
agent_decided.component: typed-decision thresholds (write gate, recall gate, routing)
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: which field of a Jev response our threshold code reads, and whether thresholds are refit locally before any gate ships

decision_chain.reason: The card defines Jev's `confidence` as (K*p_max-1)/(K-1). For a fixed option count K that is a monotone function of the top-class probability, so arms A and B admit the same decisions in the same order and have identical coverage at any error rate. What is left is whether a local refit beats raw top-class probabilities, and that is exactly E-20260926-03-r2's arms (raw vs isotonic, per source). The note's builder report (0.12 vs 0.19, one task, no code or version) is carried there as context. Until then, E-20260929-02 and E-20260929-03 read option probabilities, not `confidence`, and confirming the identity takes one logged response per K, not an experiment.

lineage.label: Jev ships two confidence numbers; the API hands you the worse one (Harrison Guo)

agent_decided.claim: On our agent tasks, serving 2 memory entries per step instead of our current top-k cuts injected memory tokens by at least 25% with a pass-rate loss of no more than 2 points.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Frozen agent harness, model and memory store. Arms: (A) current top-k; (B) top-2; (C) sufficiency stop rule where available (links H8 and B9, so the three budgets are compared once). Attribution: render each step's prompt with and without memory and count the difference (the paper's two-pass method), splitting cached and uncached input. Dataset: at least 60 tasks from our engineering-agent task set, 3 seeds per arm. Metrics: injected memory tokens and dollars per task, pass rate with bootstrap intervals by task. Predeclared margin: B adopted if injected tokens fall at least 25% and the pass-rate interval lower bound is above minus 2 points. Kill: pass rate falls more than 2 points. Note from the source: its "almost no accuracy cost" was 0.600 to 0.570 on one seed with keyword grading, so the margin here is stricter.
agent_decided.plain_title: Giving agents fewer stored notes cut memory's share of the bill by a quarter in one test.
agent_decided.why_it_matters: R3 asks for sufficient evidence within a bounded budget; the paper puts memory injection at 13.6% of variable workflow cost and growing with depth, so the default budget is a real cost lever. Exact per-step attribution is also cheap telemetry we lack today (R6).
agent_decided.component: context assembly budget for served memory
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: the default number of memory entries served per step, and whether we attribute injected-memory cost per step in our telemetry

decision_chain.reason: Not our workload and no testable margin: the note (N-20260928-28) grades applicability low (within-task buffer of upstream DAG outputs, not long-term memory, no prompt caching), the accuracy side is one seed with keyword grading (0.600 vs 0.570), fewer served entries cutting tokens is arithmetic, and 60 tasks x 3 seeds cannot resolve a 2-point pass-rate margin. The real question, fewer served entries at equal accuracy, is H8's (fixed k versus stop rule), which can report a k = 2 row; two-pass attribution of injected tokens is telemetry for P3, not an experiment.

lineage.label: Total Cost of Agency: Exact Attribution of Memory Injection Cost in Multi-Agent LLM Workflows (arXiv 2609.23790)

agent_decided.claim: On our own served-memory lines with planted instructions, a Jev injection gate blocks at least 85% of planted lines at a false-block rate at or below 5%, and a self-hosted open-weight detector does not match it.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Frozen memory store and serving path. Arms: (A) the jevmem-style single injection question at threshold 0.5; (B) the hermes-firewall two-question Jev policy as pinned at 7c5a326; (C) SemIf Qwen3.5-4B self-hosted; (D) no gate, framing only ("facts, not instructions"). Dataset: at least 150 benign memory lines sampled from our store plus at least 150 planted lines written by a person who has not seen the detectors, including instructions phrased as ordinary process (the two jevmem misses) and instructions inside quoted emails (where Laya and DeBERTa were near chance). Metrics: block rate on planted lines, false-block rate on benign lines with the rule-of-three bound (B21), cost per 1,000 lines, latency. Predeclared margin: adopt the cheapest arm whose block rate is at least 85% and whose false-block upper bound is at most 5%. Kill: no arm meets both; then the gate stays advisory and permissions carry the boundary (B25). The detector never becomes the security boundary; this card measures a filter, not authority.
agent_decided.plain_title: Jev caught nine in ten planted attacks in a public test; would it guard our stored memories?
agent_decided.why_it_matters: B24 rests on 44 author-written lines; this public 718-item result is the first larger check and shows a nonzero false-block rate (3.5%) that matters for build-time reads. The test settles which detector sits at the safety stage and whether a self-hosted option is good enough to keep memory text in-house (R8, R9).
agent_decided.component: injection gate on served memory
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: which detector guards stored memory before it is served (Jev single question, Jev two-question policy, or a self-hosted open-weight model), and what false-block rate we accept

decision_chain.reason: Same claim as register H10 (H10b): block rate and false-block rate of an injection gate on served memory lines with planted instructions, where H10b's bound is stricter (false-block upper bound at most 2% on at least 149 benign lines) than the card's 5%. When H10b is specified, add the card's arms (hermes-firewall two-question Jev policy at 7c5a326 and self-hosted SemIf Qwen3.5-4B) and its planted-email and ordinary-process wording families, citing N-20260928-35; the card's no-gate framing arm is already E-20260926-08-r2.

lineage.label: hermes-firewall: a Jev-based prompt-injection gate for an agent, benchmarked against Laya, SemIf, DeBERTa and regex

agent_decided.claim: On our coding-agent tasks, serving a short structured record written when a past task closes (bug class, root cause, fix pattern, lesson) raises the pass rate over memory-off, while serving the top-1 raw transcript chunk from the same history does not.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Frozen coding-agent harness and model, same history of past trajectories, same context budget. Arms: (A) memory off; (B) top-1 raw transcript chunk retrieved from past trajectories by our current retriever; (C) top-1 four-field record (bug class, root cause, fix pattern, reusable lesson) written by a fixed model at trajectory close, without any knowledge of future target tasks (the paper's record was target-aware, which we must not copy); (D) irrelevant record control. Dataset: at least 100 repository tasks from our own repos or SWE-style tasks with executable tests, with at least one related past trajectory each, 4 seeds per task. Metrics: pass rate by executable tests, steps and tokens per task, bootstrap intervals by task. Predeclared margin: C beats A by at least 3 points with the task-bootstrap 95% interval above zero. Kill: C does not beat A (interval includes zero) and does not reduce steps; then procedural memory stays deferred (B16 unchanged). Also record, per failing task, whether the relevant past trajectory was retrieved but its fix pattern was lost (the paper's form-degradation category) to check where B fails.
agent_decided.plain_title: Most memory tools did not make coding agents fix more bugs; how we store lessons may matter more.
agent_decided.why_it_matters: This is R6 evidence on our own workload: the paper finds that four memory systems, including Mem0, rarely beat memory-off on coding and that the served record's form, not ranking, is the main failure, which qualifies B16 (raw beats distilled). The result decides whether R5 procedural memory is worth building now and what the write step must produce.
agent_decided.component: experience memory for coding agents (record format at write time, served context)
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: whether our coding-agent memory stores raw trajectory chunks or a short structured lesson record per closed task, and whether serving either beats no memory at all

decision_chain.reason: Cannot run this quarter within POLICY-v1: an executable-test coding-agent comparison uses about 2M solver input tokens per task in the source (glm-5, N-20260928-20), so 100 tasks x 4 seeds x 4 arms needs roughly 3 billion tokens against a 2M-token, 25 USD per-run cap and 150 USD a week, and any sample small enough to fit cannot resolve the 3-point margin (the source's intervals at 444 runs per arm were about +/- 5 points); the note also marks the positive arm as target-aware and selection-biased, and procedural memory is parked in the operating plan. Re-raise if the policy budget grows or if a cheap non-agent proxy (record-level fix-pattern retention) is proposed; the B16 question stays open.

lineage.label: VibeMemBench: Evaluating Memory Systems for Coding Agents on Real Repository Coding Tasks (arXiv 2609.23570)

agent_decided.claim: Per-question isotonic calibration of Jev probabilities, fitted on our own labelled memory decisions, reduces expected calibration error by at least half on held-out decisions without lowering gate F1 by more than 1 point at validated cutoffs.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Arm A = raw Jev probabilities for the store/skip and still-true questions with the cutoff chosen on validation; arm B = the same saved Jev outputs passed through a per-question isotonic curve fitted on a training split, with its own cutoff chosen on validation. Dataset: 1,500 or more human-labelled memory decisions from our traffic, split by repository into train, validation and test. Metrics: ECE (15 bins), Brier, log loss, F1 and precision at the chosen cutoff, escalation rate at a fixed precision target. Predeclared margin: ECE reduced by 50% or more with a repository-clustered bootstrap interval excluding 0, and F1 within 1.0 point of arm A. Kill: ECE reduction under 25%, or F1 loss over 1.0 point.
agent_decided.plain_title: Can we trust our fast decision model's confidence scores? Tuning them on our own labels may fix that.
agent_decided.why_it_matters:
R9 asks whether Jev is the right System One model at the write gate; a threshold that means what it says is a precondition for setting escalation budgets and for comparing Jev with open-weight models fairly. The TRIVIA+ result suggests calibration fixes meaning, not accuracy, and the gate design should know which.
---
agent_decided.component: Jev-based write gate and staleness check thresholds
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: whether gate thresholds are set on raw Jev probabilities (fixed 0.5 or hand-picked) or on per-question isotonic-calibrated probabilities with cutoffs fitted on held-out labels

decision_chain.reason: Same claim and same arms as open spec E-20260926-03-r2 (raw versus cross-fitted isotonic recalibration of the saved save/skip gate probabilities, ECE at least 2x lower, held-out, with the selection metric reported as a check); the card's still-true question and its TRIVIA+ evidence (N-20260928-16: ECE 0.098 to 0.031, F1 unchanged at validated cutoffs, worse at a reused 0.5 cutoff) should be attached to that spec at its next revision, including the rule that a calibrated score gets its own validated cutoff.

lineage.label: Typed Evals (TrustifAI/typed_evals): Jev as a judge, calibrated against human labels on TRIVIA+

agent_decided.claim: On bug-fix tasks whose correct fix depends on a past decision recorded only in earlier sessions or decision records, a coding agent with a prompt-time memory hook needs at least 30% fewer corrections to pass a hidden test than the same agent with that history merely reachable on disk.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Arm A = coding agent (one fixed agent and model) with the history reachable but not pointed at; arm B = same agent with our memory hook injecting recalled decisions at prompt submit; optional arm C = Hindsight's coding-agents plugin as an external reference. Dataset: 40 or more tasks built from our own repositories in the sdebench pattern (a past decision on a limit, invariant, ordering or mapping; a bug report whose obvious fix contradicts it; a hidden test), plus 10 reversed-decision tasks where the recalled decision is stale. Metric: interventions to pass (cap 5), cost, turns; stale-decision tasks scored separately. Predeclared margin: B reduces total interventions by at least 30% vs A over 3 repeats, with a task-clustered bootstrap interval excluding 0, and B is not worse than A on the reversed-decision tasks by more than 1 intervention per 10 tasks. Kill: reduction under 15%, or B worse on reversed-decision tasks beyond the margin.
agent_decided.plain_title: Does remembering past decisions halve the corrections coding agents need? One vendor says yes.
agent_decided.why_it_matters:
R6 needs a benchmark that measures memory where engineering agents feel it (corrections avoided, cost), and the only data so far is vendor-planted; our own tasks give an independent check. It also tests the R5 risk that recalled decisions go stale, which the vendor benchmark omits.
---
agent_decided.component: PDLC memory benchmark (coding-agent track) and the read-path memory hook
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: whether the PDLC memory benchmark adopts "interventions to a passing hidden test" on decision-dependent bug fixes as a primary metric, and whether our memory hook is evaluated on it before any retrieval tuning

decision_chain.reason: deferred by portfolio: building 50 decision-dependent bug-fix tasks with hidden tests on our repositories and 3 repeats per arm is the most expensive test in this batch, it moves no register belief, and its only evidence is vendor-planted (52 of 61 tasks planted, task files absent from the clone, no intervals); H1 answers memory versus no memory on SE tasks first. Re-raise when the PDLC memory benchmark v1 task set exists, keeping the card's two good ideas for that scoping: interventions to a passing hidden test as the metric (solve rate saturates at 60 or 61 of 61) and reversed-decision tasks that penalise stale recall.

lineage.label: Agent Memory Benchmark (AMB, Vectorize): sdebench, does memory help a coding agent? Hindsight vs no memory

agent_decided.claim: Where a memory-poisoning defense sits predicts its benign cost: write-time defenses showed 0.000 false quarantine rate on attack-free traffic while a read-time quarantine defense falsely quarantined 33.6 % of legitimate memories (arXiv 2609.22818). Separately, a write-time prompt rule cut injection into Claude Code memory for image and PDF carriers but not text (ISR 96.7 % to 84.4 %) and did nothing once memory was poisoned (C-ASR 96.7 % to 96.7 %) (arXiv 2609.13889). Neither placement alone is shown to be sufficient.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment: Refines H10(b), which tests only a serving-path gate. Same planted set (about 40 instruction-bearing lines, add PMPA-style "store this rule" payloads arriving via tool results, text carrier) and a benign set of at least 149 independent engineering memories from real project history. Three arms, same classifier and threshold: (A) gate at extraction write time; (B) gate at serving time (current H10b); (C) both. Metrics: planted lines served (block rate), benign false-block rate with one-sided 95 % upper bound, served tokens, p95 serving latency, and for arm A the rate at which poisoned lines already in the store before the gate was enabled are still served. Kill for A as a replacement for B: A leaves pre-existing poisoned lines served. Kill for B: false-block upper bound above 2 % (H10's own threshold).
agent_decided.plain_title: Protecting customers from planted instructions in memory: checking at read time wrongly blocked one good memory in three.
agent_decided.why_it_matters: B24 rests on 44 author-written lines with one placement. The external evidence says benign cost depends on placement and that write-only defenses cannot repair an already poisoned store, so the choice of placement is the decision, not just the classifier threshold.
agent_decided.component: extraction consumer write path and /v1/context serving path
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: whether the B5 injection gate runs at write time, at serve time, or both

decision_chain.reason: The evidence does not support the card's paper-ablated placement claim: in N-SURVEY-20260928-01 placement is confounded with mechanism (write-time sanitize, provenance and anomaly checks vs a read-time contradiction-quarantine reranker, which the note says does not transfer to an injection classifier), and N-SURVEY-20260928-03's defense is a prompt rule, so no source isolates placement of the same classifier; arm A's kill (pre-existing poisoned lines still served) holds by construction and needs no run. The residual question, same classifier and threshold at write time vs serve time on the same benign lines, is cheapest answered as an added arm on E-20260926-08-r2, whose 150 benign lines already bound false blocks near 2 percent; re-raise it at that spec's next revision.

lineage.label: The Price of Safety: Benign-Case Utility and Token Overhead of Memory-Poisoning Defenses in LLM Agents

agent_decided.claim: No public memory benchmark grades the questions a product-development memory must answer (decision reasons weeks later, superseded requirements, PR-to-requirement links, repeated failed fixes, stale memories, abstention) on real engineering history. LoCoMo is near saturation with a 6.4 % wrong answer key and a lenient grader; LongMemEval self-reports cluster at 89 to 95 %; DolphinBench grades office actions on synthetic personas; CL-Bench has 19 bug-fix issues and no requirements; DreamBench-SWE covers multi-session coding only. A benchmark of our own is the only way to test the PDLC layer's claims. This is a design opinion; nothing is measured yet.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment:
Build v1 of the PDLC memory benchmark and run it once.
- Task families (6): F1 decision and its reason weeks later; F2 requirement changed, older statements superseded; F3 link a PR to the requirement it implements, with a planted plausible wrong candidate; F4 warn before repeating a failed fix; F5 spot a stale memory after the code under it changed; F6 abstain when memory has nothing.
- Items: 60 scored items per family (360) plus 120 benign controls for F4 and F5, 480 in total; half from our own repository, issues, PRs, design docs and session transcripts (private split), half from public spec-driven repositories in SpecMine's Kiro and PR layers (published split). Gold drafted from artifact structure (closing keywords, typed references, reverts, content hashes), verified by two annotators with 30 % double labelling; every item must pass with evidence and fail without history (DolphinBench validity filter).
- Systems: Engram (ledger-only and graph), Mem0 OSS, Zep (Graphiti OSS), Letta, Hindsight, supermemory if its terms allow, a no-memory reader and a full-context reader; same reader model throughout, three runs each, cost and p50/p95 latency per query. Then swap the decider at one memory stage at a time (linking, recall gate, staleness, pre-action warning) between an LLM, Jev and an open-weight System One model.
- Useful if: system rankings on our items differ materially from rankings on LongMemEval and DolphinBench for the same systems, or at least two families separate systems by more than the noise floor with paired intervals excluding zero, and at least one stage swap gives a decision we would act on.
- Kill: if system rankings on our items agree with public-benchmark rankings (Kendall tau at least 0.8 over the systems run on both) and no family separates systems beyond the noise floor, ours adds nothing and we stop at v1 and use the public ones. Also stop and redesign if the validity filter rejects more than half of any family's items (the questions are answerable without memory).
- Size of effort: about 8 weeks of one engineer after the eval-harness fixes, about 160 annotator hours, roughly USD 3,000 to 8,000 of model spend (estimate), most of it on the full-context rows.
agent_decided.plain_title: Can we prove our memory beats Mem0 and Zep for software teams? Few public tests check this.
agent_decided.why_it_matters: Priority 4 in the CTO's list. Every PDLC-layer decision in the discovery plan (typed supersession, trace links, staleness audits, the pre-action gate, where Jev sits) is currently judged on chat-memory tests that do not contain these questions, and our own harness leaked labels. Without this benchmark we cannot say to a customer that Engram helps their engineers more than Mem0 or Zep, and we cannot tell which memory stages are worth a System One model. If the kill criterion fires, we save the effort of maintaining a benchmark and lean on public ones.
agent_decided.component: evaluation harness (replaces tests/eval per P3) and the PDLC memory layer
agent_decided.decision_it_could_change: whether we claim, and publish, that Engram's PDLC memory beats Mem0, Zep, Letta and Hindsight on engineering work, and at which memory stages a System One model replaces an LLM

decision_chain.reason: deferred by portfolio: a cost L, opinion-grade design scope (8 engineer-weeks, about 160 annotator hours, USD 3,000 to 8,000) cannot be sized while policy is unset, its Engram rows are blocked by P1 to P3, and its own note leaves seven CTO questions open (dogfood corpus and transcript use, publication, supermemory terms, reproducer, full-context budget, stage swaps in v1) that decide the spec; its Kendall-tau kill over about five systems is also too coarse to falsify. Re-raise after the CTO answers those questions and after E-20260928-08 (its 300 labelled SpecMine pairs seed family F3), as a narrowed v0 of families F2, F3 and F5 on the public split with competitors run first, as the note itself recommends.

lineage.label: Scope: our own memory test for product-development work (PDLC memory benchmark, v1)

agent_decided.claim: SkillEvolBench ran 180 tasks across 6 environments with 10 models and 3 CLIs (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI). Under frozen deployment, skills revised only after failures scored -2.56 pp vs no-skill (1 win, 1 tie, 8 losses), and curated static skills scored -2.44 pp. Raw-trajectory reuse scored 37.6% ESR vs a computed no-skill mean of 34.7%, above every skill arm's mean. Only update-after-every-attempt arms were slightly positive (+0.78 and +0.44 pp). Replay success overstated transfer by up to about 18 pp. Separately, HGM found that a lineage-pooled signal predicted descendants' performance better than an agent's own score (weighted r 0.778 vs 0.285 for DGM and 0.444 for SICA on SWE-Verified-60). HGM ran once, with no ablation separating the lineage signal from its other changes.
agent_decided.proposed_experiment:
This refines H6 and H3. H6 compares one-episode with multi-episode induction and scores re-use on the same `task_key`. This card adds the update-policy axis and a split of the held-out set.
Arms, on the H6 episode set:
- Arm A: raw top-3 episodes (no induction).
- Arm B: Workflow induced once, then frozen.
- Arm C: Workflow revised only after failures.
- Arm D: Workflow revised after every reuse.
Score on held-out variants split into three kinds:
- context shift
- adversarial shortcut (a tempting instance-specific path that is wrong)

proposed_undecided.proposed_experiment: Refines H3 (read-time curation vs write-time summaries) and H1 (raw ledger floor) by adding the arm this paper tested, on engineering history instead of chat. Data: the H1 DreamBench-SWE sequences plus 150 PDLC questions from the scoped PDLC benchmark (decision behind a design, changed requirement, which PR implements what). Arms at two predeclared budgets (about 300 and about 1,500 served tokens): (A) raw ledger events, BM25+embedding shortlist of 30, no selector; (B) A plus one Jev Noul per shortlisted event with the paper's option wording, top k by probability; (C) A plus the same Noul on a self-hosted open-weight model (Jev-Style-2B or Laya) and a label log-probability arm on an open backbone, per the audit checklist in N-SURVEY-20260929-05; (D) our current LLM extraction at write time, retrieved the same way. Recall/no-recall gate held fixed and separate in every arm. Metrics: oracle pass count or exact-answer accuracy with a judge from a different model family than the answerer; write cost per 1,000 events; read p50 and p95; evidence-dropped rate; abstention on unanswerable questions. Kill for replacing extraction: B more than 3 points below D at the small budget, or B's evidence-dropped rate above 10% on PDLC questions.
proposed_undecided.plain_title: Can we stop paying to summarise everything we store, and just pick the right raw notes later?
proposed_undecided.why_it_matters: Paying a large model to summarise everything we store is the biggest running cost of memory and sends customer text to an outside model. One careful test says a cheap decision model can pick the right raw notes at answer time just as well, for a tiny fraction of the cost, when little context is handed over. If that holds on engineering work, we can drop most write-time extraction, keep exact original text for audits, and run the picker ourselves.
proposed_undecided.component: ingestion pipeline (Consumer extraction) and the read path rerank step
proposed_undecided.decision_it_could_change: whether Engram extracts facts with an LLM at write time for engineering history, or stores raw events and selects with a System One model at read time

lineage.label: When Does Selection Replace Extraction? A Pre-Registered Test of Agent Memory with a Typed Decision Model (arXiv 2609.34227)

proposed_undecided.claim: On 3,103 issues and 7,688 commits across six large projects, a LightGBM LambdaMART ranker over text similarity plus six metadata features (time proximity, diff size, file overlap and others) reached average F1 73.17 on issue-to-commit links against 48.39 for a GPT-OSS-120B agent and 35.88 for SBERT plus GPT-4o rerank, in 19.6 vs 421 minutes of test time (arXiv 2607.23610). Metadata was the largest single contributor (PyTorch: all features 76.38, SBERT only 44.69). A small supervised RoBERTa+GraphCodeBERT model also beat plain Gemini 2.5 Pro on requirement-to-code links (0.7155 vs 0.5874, arXiv 2509.05585). Gold links in both come from developer references, which the authors call inconsistent.
proposed_undecided.proposed_experiment: Refines PC-SURVEY-20260928-06 (Jev vs open-weight vs fine-tuned vs LLM checker on IMPLEMENTS links) by adding the arm it lacks, a no-model metadata ranker, and a cascade that spends model calls only on its top candidates; H7 then consumes the links. Data: the same 300 adjudicated (requirement or ticket, PR) pairs from 6 to 10 SpecMine Kiro repositories plus one internal repository, each requirement with its full candidate pool of PRs within +-180 days; train the ranker on a disjoint set of repositories. Arms: (A) LambdaMART over BM25, embedding cosine, time proximity, file overlap with paths named in the requirement or design, diff size; (B) Jev Noul "does this PR implement this requirement?" on every candidate; (C) A, then Jev on A's top 5; (D) A, then an LLM checker on A's top 5; (E) A, then a self-hosted open-weight decision model on A's top 5. Metrics: F1 and precision at recall 0.8 against the adjudicated labels; model calls and cost per 1,000 requirements; p95 latency. Kill for the ranker-first design: C and E both more than 3 F1 points below B, or A's top 5 missing the gold PR for more than 10% of requirements.
proposed_undecided.plain_title: Can simple clues like timing and shared files link code to requirements as well as paid models?
proposed_undecided.why_it_matters: Linking each piece of code to the requirement it delivers is the core of the product-development memory, and asking a model about every possible pair is the expensive part. A published study found that simple clues we already record, such as when things happened and which files they touched, found the right links better than large models and far faster. If that holds for us, the graph can check only a handful of candidates per requirement, which makes keeping it current on every change affordable.
proposed_undecided.component: PDLC linking stage (IMPLEMENTS edges from tickets and requirements to PRs and commits)
proposed_undecided.decision_it_could_change: whether candidate trace links are first ranked by cheap repository features before any model call, and which model (none, Jev, open-weight, LLM) makes the final call

lineage.label: Deciding trace links without a large model: LinkRank (arXiv 2607.23610), with NL-PL traceability (2509.05585), R2Code (2604.22432) and requirements quality (2606.11834, 2608.15726)

proposed_undecided.claim: In one automotive project, about 10% of human-maintained requirement links were invalid (219 of 2,132). Zero-shot Claude 3.5 Sonnet detected invalid links poorly (invalid-class F1 29.45%); giving it the 3 most similar valid and 3 most similar invalid labelled links raised invalid-F1 to 94.06% (TVR, arXiv 2504.15427), and its errors did not overlap with a plain retrieval classifier's. Across 6.7 million distinct links in commit messages, 70% no longer resolve (arXiv 2305.16591). Jev had the highest contradiction recall of ten models on a three-way entail / contradict / not-mentioned task at about one sixth to one four-hundredth of the others' cost (arXiv 2609.27678).
proposed_undecided.proposed_experiment: Refines H10(a), which audits whether stored Decisions are still true against a snapshot, by applying it to trace links, a case H10 does not cover; its first test ("no gain over source-change invalidation") is arm A here. Data: 200 IMPLEMENTS and REFINES links from SpecMine repositories where the requirement or design file, or the linked code, changed after the link was made, plus 100 links whose ends did not change; two labellers mark each link still valid / no longer valid after the change, kappa reported; rejected links from a disjoint repository set form the labelled-neighbour pool. Arms: (A) source-change invalidation: flag every link whose end changed; (B) Jev Noul "does this PR still implement this requirement as now written?" zero-shot, threshold fit with one temperature on a held-out half (N-SURVEY-20260929-02); (C) B with the 3 most similar valid and 3 most similar invalid labelled links placed in the state; (D) an LLM with the same 3+3 neighbours (TVR recipe); (E) C then D below a confidence threshold. Metrics: invalid-link precision at recall 0.7, invalid-class F1, false-flag rate on unchanged links, cost per 1,000 checks. Kill for model-based revalidation: no arm beats A by 0.10 precision at recall 0.7.
proposed_undecided.plain_title: When a requirement or its code changes, can we tell which of our links went wrong?
proposed_undecided.why_it_matters: The links in our product-development memory will be imported from tools and made by models, and published studies show about one in ten such links is wrong, and many more go bad as documents and code change. An agent that trusts a wrong link will act on the wrong requirement. This test tells us whether a cheap check can catch broken links when something changes, or whether simply flagging every changed link for review is just as good.
proposed_undecided.component: PDLC linking stage, link maintenance job (Consumer 4 or an on-change hook)
proposed_undecided.decision_it_could_change: whether a trace link is re-checked when either end changes, and whether that check is a rule, Jev, Jev with labelled neighbours, or an LLM

lineage.label: Existing trace links are often wrong or dead: TVR link validation (arXiv 2504.15427), with link decay in commit messages (arXiv 2305.16591) and ADR mining (arXiv 2609.07375)

proposed_undecided.claim: On declarative low-trust edits that consolidation turns into procedures, a dispatch-time check that blocks protected actions unless their triggering memory traces to an authorised source cuts unauthorised protected actions to at most one third of the rate left by an instruction-detecting injection gate alone, while keeping legitimate-action success within 5 points (paper: 2.0% vs 13.7% for write-time update checking, legitimate success 92.1% vs 95.9% undefended, Table 6).
proposed_undecided.proposed_experiment: Arm A = our memory stack with only the instruction-detecting injection gate on served lines (current B5 design). Arm B = the same stack plus a registry of protected actions (merge, deploy, requirement or spec status change) and a dispatch-time check that requires every memory record that justified the action to carry provenance to an authorised source, with provenance propagated through consolidated records. Dataset: 40 to 60 fixtures built from our own PDLC traces, each with one declarative edit planted in a low-trust source (issue comment, PR description, CI log) designed to be consolidated and retrieved on a later clean task, plus an equal number of clean tasks that legitimately need a protected action. Metric: memory-path unauthorised-action rate (counted only when the action is traced to the planted record), legitimate protected-action success, added latency. Predeclared margin: Arm B unauthorised rate at most one third of Arm A and legitimate success drop of at most 5 points. Kill: if Arm A already blocks at least 90% of planted edits, or Arm B costs more than 10 points of legitimate success, drop the dispatch check.
proposed_undecided.plain_title: A planted note in a ticket can make our agent merge or deploy. Is our current filter enough to stop it?
proposed_undecided.why_it_matters: R8 says evidence cannot authorise its own execution; this tests whether our read-time injection gate enforces that for consolidated memory or whether authority must be checked where actions are dispatched. The paper shows declarative edits pass instruction detectors, which is exactly the shape of stale or planted facts in engineering tickets.
proposed_undecided.component: safety gate on served and consolidated memory; protected-action registry
proposed_undecided.decision_it_could_change: whether our B5 injection gate is enough, or protected actions (merge, deploy, spec status change) need a dispatch-time provenance check

lineage.label: BMA: Backchain Memory Attacks Create Unauthorized Control Paths in LLM Agents

proposed_undecided.claim: Serving superseded values with explicit validity dates (supersede-and-retain) raises previous-value accuracy by at least 15 points over hiding them (supersede-and-hide) while costing no more than 3 points of current-value accuracy, and the overall accuracy of the two arms differs by less than the previous-value gap (the MemProbe pattern: Graphiti vs LangMem tied overall, p>0.37, previous-value 96.4 vs 67.9, p=0.002).
proposed_undecided.proposed_experiment: Arm A = our store with supersede-and-hide (only the current value is served). Arm B = same store with supersede-and-retain (old and new values served, each with valid-from and valid-to and a supersedes link). Same reader model, same retrieval budget, same extraction. Dataset: MemProbe suite56 through its adapter interface, plus 30 PDLC episodes built with its authoring kit in which a requirement, design decision or constraint changes mid-history. Metric: current-value accuracy, previous-value accuracy and change-detection accuracy reported separately, typed-field scoring against gold, paired bootstrap over episodes with 3 runs per arm. Predeclared margin: previous-value gain at least 15 points with current-value loss at most 3 points. Kill: if Arm B loses more than 3 points on current value, or the previous-value gain is under 5 points, keep hide as default and drop retain.
proposed_undecided.plain_title: When a requirement changes, should the agent still see the old version, clearly dated? Accuracy alone can hide the answer.
proposed_undecided.why_it_matters: R2 asks for distinct semantics for supersession; engineering agents need both "what is the requirement now" and "what did we decide before and why", and B3 cannot be tested with a single accuracy number. This card also fixes a scoring rule for our PDLC memory benchmark (priority 4): report the stability and plasticity sides separately.
proposed_undecided.component: supersession policy and read surface of the memory store
proposed_undecided.decision_it_could_change: whether superseded memories are hidden from the reader or served with validity dates, and whether our PDLC memory benchmark reports current-value and previous-value accuracy separately

lineage.label: MemProbe: stability-plasticity diagnostics for six incremental memory systems (Mem0, Zep/Graphiti, LangMem, Cognee, A-MEM, MemoryOS; Letta and Hindsight excluded)

proposed_undecided.claim: On our own write-gate and linking decisions, local Laya served through Unsloth's Jev-compatible API, with thresholds refit on its `probabilities` output, reaches within 3 points of hosted Jev on precision at the automation threshold at no more than 2x its p50 latency on a CPU host.
proposed_undecided.proposed_experiment: Arm A = hosted Jev (jev-latest) through the TypeSafe SDK with our current thresholds. Arm B = the same SDK with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at Unsloth's local /v1/systemone serving Laya (English typed-decisions variant for 512-token units, Multilingual for up to 1024), thresholds refit on `probabilities` (not `confidence`, whose formula differs) on a dev split. Identical questions (noul, choice with at most 20 described options, score). Dataset: 300 labelled PDLC decisions (150 write-gate save or skip, 150 link or supersede decisions between requirement, design and ticket units), each under 1024 tokens, split 100 dev and 200 test. Metric: precision and coverage at the automation threshold, macro accuracy, p50 and p95 latency, 400 and 422 rejection rate. Predeclared margin: Arm B precision within 3 points of Arm A at equal or higher coverage. Kill: if Arm B is more than 5 points worse at matched coverage, or more than 5% of real units exceed the context window, keep hosted Jev and record the gap.
proposed_undecided.plain_title: Can we keep project memory on our own machines and still decide what to store as well as today?
proposed_undecided.why_it_matters: Priority 2 is running a decision model ourselves so memory text stays in-house; this is the cheapest possible test because the swap is a base URL change on the SDK we already use. It measures R9 quality at the two stages where the field has no evidence, and records the compatibility gaps (confidence formula, option trimming, context limit) before anyone builds on them.
proposed_undecided.component: System One decision model at the write gate and linking stage
proposed_undecided.decision_it_could_change: whether memory text can stay in-house by running Laya locally at the write gate and linking stage instead of hosted Jev

lineage.label: Unsloth Decision API: serving Laya locally behind a TypeSafe/Jev-compatible endpoint

proposed_undecided.claim: On build-time tasks whose MCP results exceed 100 KB, a Jev relevance hook that keeps only relevant segments (pass-through when the best score is below 0.5, 6,000-byte packet, verbatim recovery by id) cuts agent wall time by at least 20% and total cost including Jev tokens by at least 10% with no drop in task correctness.
proposed_undecided.proposed_experiment: Arm A = Claude Code with its normal handling of oversized MCP results (no hook). Arm B = the same agent with the JevScout hook at commit a42e81b, default thresholds. Same model, same prompts, same tools. Dataset: 12 build-time tasks from our PDLC work that return large results (multi-hundred-comment tickets, long Confluence design pages, big search responses), 5 runs per task per arm. Metric: task correctness graded blind against a per-task rubric by two reviewers, wall time, total cost including TypeSafe charges, count of recovery calls. Predeclared margin: time down at least 20% and cost down at least 10% with correctness not lower by more than 1 run in 60. Kill: if correctness drops by 2 or more runs in 60 or total cost including Jev tokens does not fall, drop the hook.
proposed_undecided.plain_title: Can a cheap filter trim huge tool outputs so our coding agent finishes faster without more mistakes?
proposed_undecided.why_it_matters: R3 asks for sufficient evidence within a bounded budget; this is a cheap, reversible assembly-stage test of a System One filter on exactly our build-time read pattern (priority 1). The author's report omits Jev token cost and half its tasks, so our own run is the only way to know whether the saving is real.
proposed_undecided.component: context assembly for tool results at build time
proposed_undecided.decision_it_could_change: whether to prune oversized tool results with a System One relevance filter (with pass-through below 0.5 and verbatim recovery) before they reach the coding agent

# The CTO's research priorities (in order)

Every agent reads this. Priority topics are examined in full (no budget cut), get notes for credible usage reports even when no test is implied, and get reserved recommendation slots. Change this file to change what the loop pays attention to.

## 1. System One models across the memory stages
Jev and other System One models at every memory stage, starting with ingestion, reranking and retrieval of the context graph, then deciding what to store, linking, and deciding whether to recall. Want: who uses them where, with what results; our own tests at the stages where the field has no evidence (ingestion, linking, retrieval of the graph).
Pillars: R9 (primary), R3, R10. Match terms: Jev, TypeSafe, System One, System-One, typed decision, Noul, decision model.

## 2. Open-weight System One models, both as a goal and as a comparison
Goal: be able to run a decision model ourselves so memory text stays in-house, and tune it on our own decisions. Comparison: Jev against open-weight models (Laya and its ports, Intern-Decision, this-that-model, semif, CLM, successors) on our own decisions: quality, cost, latency, hardware, licence.
Pillars: R9. Match terms: open weight(s), open-source decision model, Laya, Intern-Decision, this-that-model, FLock, semif, CLM, distil(l), self-host, GGUF, MLX.

## 3. The PDLC ontology
Evolve the context graph's ontology for the product development lifecycle: first-class artifacts (requirement, design section, decision, constraint, ticket, pull request, test), claims anchored to exact content, confidence-scored trace links (implements, verifies, refines, satisfies, blocks), outcomes fed back, a check before an agent acts. Starting point: docs/research/2026-09/pdlc-memory-layer.md. Narrow slice this quarter, tested with a System One model deciding the links.
Pillars: R10 (primary), R9, R2. Match terms: ontology, schema evolution, knowledge graph schema, context graph, traceability, trace link, trace-link, PDLC, node type.

## 4. Memory benchmarks, including scoping our own PDLC memory benchmark
A living map of what each memory benchmark measures and whether it reflects engineering-agent work (LongMemEval, LoCoMo, DolphinBench, CL-Bench and new ones). Scope our own PDLC memory benchmark: recall the decision behind a design weeks later, notice a changed requirement, link a pull request to what it implements, warn before repeating a failed fix, spot a stale memory.
Pillars: R6 (primary), R10. Match terms: LongMemEval, LoCoMo, DolphinBench, CL-Bench, memory benchmark, memory-benchmark, PDLC memory benchmark.

## How agents apply this
- Triage: every cluster matching a priority's terms is examined, whatever its engagement. A credible usage report on a priority topic gets a note even without an implied test. Notes and cards carry `priority: 1..4` when they match.
- Survey: R9 and R10 get three of the fourteen weekly slots each; a monthly benchmark sweep; each run states which priority it served.
- Hypotheses: two of the five weekly recommendation slots are reserved for priority topics, in priority order, when a qualifying card exists.
- Briefs and the desk: a card on a priority topic says so in plain words; the desk shows a "System One map" and filters by priority.

# Research pillars v2 and the memory-stage lens

Every agent in the research loop labels notes, cards and specs with ONE primary pillar (by the claim being tested, not by whether it agrees with us), optional secondary pillars, and ONE memory stage. Pillars are topics, not beliefs; beliefs live in beliefs.md.

## Pillars

| Id | Pillar | Thesis | Boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Evidence and reproducibility | Decisions need identifiable source evidence and an explicit replay guarantee | evidence identity and preservation; what was served and can it be reproduced |
| R2 | State evolution and lifecycle | Updates, supersession, consolidation and retirement need distinct semantics | durable state changes to memory: write gates, supersession, consolidation mechanisms, retention, suppression, erasure |
| R3 | Retrieval and context assembly | Select sufficient authorised evidence within a bounded budget | request-time evidence selection: hybrid retrieval, traversal, curation, stopping, budgets |
| R4 | Decision quality and abstention | Automate a decision only when its error costs and uncertainty are understood | rules, classifiers, NLI, rerankers, larger models and human review as candidate implementations; abstention; calibration; escalation (the model-agnostic question of WHEN to automate) |
| R5 | Learning from experience | Outcomes may improve future behaviour if attribution and transfer are valid | receipts joined to outcomes, negative evidence, procedure induction, transfer, harmful reinforcement, self-improvement levels |
| R6 | Evaluation and research integrity | Conclusions require traceable protocols, independent checks and uncertainty | whether an evaluation supports its conclusion: leakage, judge bias, statistics, cost accounting, replication; memory benchmarks, including our own PDLC memory benchmark |
| R7 | Interoperability and coordination contracts | Agents and stores need explicit, testable exchange and capability semantics | cross-store compatibility: interfaces, registries, replay levels, swap tests, mappings, multi-agent handoff contracts |
| R8 | Trust and governance | Evidence cannot authorise its own use, execution or promotion | identity, permissions, suppression, poisoned or injected evidence, execution authority, review ownership, recovery |
| R9 | System One decision models | A fast typed decision model belongs at a memory stage only where it measurably beats the alternative on our data, at a cost and privacy we accept | which System One model (hosted: Jev; open-weight: Laya, Intern-Decision, this-that-model, semif, CLM and successors) sits at which memory stage; quality on our workload; cost and latency; self-hosting and keeping memory text in-house; fine-tuning on our own decisions; failure modes |
| R10 | The context graph and its ontology | The graph's schema and its links are product decisions that must be tested, not assumed | ingesting material and placing it on node types; linking (supersedes, contradicts, and the PDLC trace links implements, verifies, refines, satisfies, blocks) with confidence; anchoring claims to exact content; evolving the schema; traversal at retrieval time; first agenda: the PDLC artifacts and trace links |

R4 versus R9: R4 asks when any decision should be automated; R9 asks whether System One models specifically are the right implementation at each stage. A Jev calibration study is R9 primary, R4 secondary.

## Memory stages (the lens; tag every note, card and spec with one)

| Stage id | Stage |
|---|---|
| ingestion | Ingesting material into memory: extraction, chunking, placing on node types |
| write_gate | Deciding whether to store something at all |
| linking | Linking memories into the graph: duplicates, contradictions, one fact replacing another, trace links |
| consolidation | Merging, summarising and forgetting over time |
| recall_gate | Deciding whether to recall memory at all for a request |
| routing | Choosing which store, view, tool or AI handles a request |
| retrieval | Retrieval and walking the context graph |
| reranking | Reranking or filtering what retrieval returns |
| assembly | Deciding how much context to hand over, and when to stop |
| staleness | Checking whether a stored memory is still true |
| safety | Blocking poisoned or injected memory; permissions |
| evaluation | Grading output; benchmarks; measuring quality |
| none | Not specific to one stage |

pillars_plain.R1: Evidence and reproducibility: can we show exactly what a decision was based on, and replay it later?
pillars_plain.R2: State evolution and lifecycle: how memories change over time: updates, one fact replacing another, merging, forgetting.
pillars_plain.R3: Retrieval and context assembly: picking the right evidence for a task within a size budget.
pillars_plain.R4: Decision quality and abstention: small fast decision models (like Jev), classifiers and rerankers: when to trust them, when to escalate, how calibrated they are.
pillars_plain.R5: Learning from experience: whether an agent actually gets better from its outcomes, and the ways that goes wrong.
pillars_plain.R6: Evaluation and research integrity: whether our numbers can be trusted: leakage, judge bias, statistics, replication.
pillars_plain.R7: Interoperability and coordination contracts: how memory systems and agents plug into each other: interfaces, vendors, federation.
pillars_plain.R8: Trust and governance: permissions, poisoned or injected memories, who may authorise what.
